question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -5 & -1 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then $l_{21}\cdot u_{12}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices: \[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -5 & -1 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \dfrac{5}{2}R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{5}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & \dfrac{3}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{5}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{5}{2} & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & \dfrac{3}{2} \end{bmatrix} }_{U}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=-\dfrac52, u_{12}=1,$ and $l_{21}\cdot u_{12}=-\dfrac52.$

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -2 & -5 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then $l_{21}+u_{22}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ -2 & -5 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] & = U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=-1,u_{22}=0,$ and $l_{21}+u_{22}=-1.$

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then $l_{21}+u_{22}=$
question.explanation:
We need to reduce the matrix to the row echelon form. For every elementary row operation we also write the equivalent notation in terms of multiplication by the corresponding elementary matrix: \[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + 2R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=-2,u_{22}=0,$ and $l_{21}+u_{22}=-2.$
